newsitem.title: UK: EU commission says euro will be reality from 1999.
newsitem.headline: EU commission says euro will be reality from 1999.

text.p: European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) has passed the point of no return and will become a reality from the start of 1999, the European Union Commissioner for monetary affairs said on Thursday.
"The euro will be a reality on January 1, 1999," Yves-Thibault de Silguy told bussinessmen at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) in London.
"I urge you to take the necessary steps to prepare, whatever the UK government decides."

Britain, which faces a general election by May 22 at the latest, remains indecisive about whether to join EMU while many European countries have vowed to enter a single currency despite the tough fiscal and economic standards required.

De Silguy reiterated that it was vital for the economic success of the single currency that the Maastricht Treaty and its rules on economic convergence was applied strictly to all participating countries.
"There is no room for fudging the figures or for cooking the books," he said. "Otherwise the euro will not inspire public confidence and market credibility."
De Silguy sought to reassure sceptical Britons that a single European currency would not mean the creation of a European super-state.
"I am not a starry-eyed federalist," he said. "There is no Franco-German plot to deprive member states of their competence for economic policy."
The Commissioner said he did not know how many countries would participate in the first wave of a single currency in 1999, adding that would be decided in a year's time.

"But I am confident that a significant number of countries will be ready," he said. "The political will is there, economic convergence is well on track and the outlook for economic growth is improving."

THe comments come against a backdrop of controversy regarding Italy's bid to be among the first wave of countries in EMU. On Wednesday, there were reports, later denied by leaders in Italy and Germany and by the European Commission, that a compromise plan for a late Italy entry was under consideration.
European member states which want to participate in a single European currency must conform to certain criteria on inflation and debt levels.
In an apparent reference to Britain's opt-out from the single currency, de Silguy said this was the freedom to remain outside, but "not the means to stop the other countries from going ahead."
He added the Commission was convinced British participation in monetary union would be good for Britain and Europe.
"Politically, Europe works best firing on all cylinders rather than having two or three countries driving the engine," he said.
"Whether the UK joins or not, the euro will have a profound effect on you and your members," de Silguy told the CBI.
He said no country in the EU wanted Brussels "interfering unnecessarily in the nooks and crannies of daily life".
"National identity is alive and well after 40 years of progress with European integration," he said.
De Silguy also calmed fears that some EMU member states may have to bear the unfunded pension liabilities of other states.
"This is nonsense. The Treaty explicitly forbids member states from bailing out each others' financial liabilities."
He said the legislative process within the EU ensured vital national interests were reflected in Community legislation.
De Silguy said London's financial community might not suffer unduly from being excluded from monetary union but it would certainly gain from being inside the euro zone from the start.
